## Variable Types and Terminologies

Symbols and variable conventions follow the rules outlined by the textbook. Input variables are denoted by the symbol $X$. If $X$ is a vector, then its components are accessed by subscripts $X_j$. Quantitative outputs are denoted by $Y$, and qualitative outputs by $G$. Observed values are written in lowercase; for example the $i$th observed value of $X$ is written as $x_i$ (where $x_i$ is a scalar or vector). Matrices are represented by bold uppercase letters; for example, a set of $N$ input $p$-vectors $x_i$, $i = 1, \ldots, N$ is represented by the $N \times p$ matrix $\mathbf{X}$. In general, vectors are not bold, except when they have $N$ components; this convention distinguishes a $p$-vector of inputs $x_i$ for the $i$th observation from the $N$-vector $\mathbf{x}_j$ consisting of all the observations on variable $X_j$. Since all vectors are assumed to be column vectors, the $i$th row of $\mathbf{X}$ is $x_i^{T}$, the vector transpose of $x_i$.

For most learning tasks, we can understand it as such: given an input vector $X$, we want to make a good prediction of the output $Y$, denoted as $\hat{Y}$. If $Y\in\mathbb{R}$ then $\hat{Y}$ too; likewise for categorical outputs, $\hat{G}$ should take values in the same set $\mathcal{G}$ associated with $G$.

For accurate prediction, data is necessary. We denote training data as a set of measurements $(x_i,y_i)$ or $(x_i,g_i)$, $i = 1,\ldots,N$.

## Prediction Approaches: Least Squares and Nearest Neighbors

Two prediction methods are explored here: The linear model fit by least squares and the $k$-nearest neighbor prediction rule.

### Linear Models and Least Squares

Given a vector of inputs $X^{T} = (X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_p)$, we predict the output $Y$ via the model:

$$
\begin{equation}
\hat{Y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{p} X_j\hat{\beta}_j
(\#eq:leq)
\end{equation}
$$

where $\hat{\beta}_0$ is the intercept. Equivalently, we can write the linear model in vector form as an inner product:

$$
\begin{equation}
\hat{Y} = X^{T}\hat{\beta}
(\#eq:leqvec)
\end{equation}
$$

where $X = \begin{pmatrix}1\\x_1\\\vdots\\x_p\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{p+1}$ and $\hat{\beta} = \begin{pmatrix}\hat{\beta}_0\\\hat{\beta}_1\\\vdots\\\hat{\beta}_p\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{p+1}$, such that $\hat{Y} = \sum_{i=0}^{p}\hat{\beta}_i x_i$.

If $\mathbf{X}$ is instead a feature matrix with $N$ samples and $p+1$ columns (the $p$ inputs together with a leading constant), so that $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times(p+1)}$, we can represent $\mathbf{X}^{T}$ as the row of column vectors $\begin{bmatrix} X_0 & X_1 & X_2 & \ldots & X_p \end{bmatrix}$, where each $X_j$ is a column vector in $\mathbb{R}^N$. For example, $X_1^T = [x_1^{(1)} \; x_1^{(2)} \; \ldots \; x_1^{(N)}]$ and $X_0$ is a constant vector of ones. Suppose further that $\hat{Y}$ is a $K$-dimensional row vector instead of a scalar; then by equation \@ref(eq:leq), $\beta$ must necessarily be a $(p+1) \times K$ matrix of coefficients.

<details>
<summary>Proposition: the linear model is a hyperplane.</summary>

::: {.proposition #prp-hyperplane}
In the $(p+1)$-dimensional input-output space, the graph $(X, \hat{Y})$ of the linear model \@ref(eq:leqvec) is a hyperplane.
:::

*Proof.* By the linear structure of equation \@ref(eq:leqvec),

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\hat{Y} &= X^{T}\beta \\
        &= \sum_{i=0}^{p} \beta_i x_i \\
        &= \beta_0 + \sum_{i=1}^p \beta_i x_i
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

Moving the intercept to the left-hand side,

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
-\beta_0 &= \sum_{i=1}^{p} \beta_i x_i - \hat{Y} \\
         &= \sum_{i=1}^p \beta_i x_i + (-1)\hat{Y} \\
         &= \begin{pmatrix}\beta_1 & \ldots & \beta_p & -1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x_1 & \ldots & x_p & \hat{Y}\end{pmatrix}^T
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

A hyperplane is defined by $\mathbf{w}^{T}\mathbf{z}= b$. Letting $\mathbf{w} = (\beta_1\ \ldots\ \beta_p\ {-1})^T$ and $\mathbf{z}=(x_1\ \ldots\ x_p\ \hat{Y})^T$, we obtain $\mathbf{w}^{T}\mathbf{z} = -\beta_0$, where the intercept $\beta_0$ translates the hyperplane away from the origin. $\qquad\square$
</details>

### Residual Sum of Squares

To fit our training data to the linear model, we use the method of least squares. We pick the coefficients $\beta$ that minimize the residual sum of square:

$$
\begin{equation}
\text{RSS}(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_i - x_{i}^{T}\beta)^2
(\#eq:RSS)
\end{equation}
$$

$\text{RSS}(\beta)$ is a quadratic function of the parameters, hence its minimum always exists but may not be unique.

<details>
<summary>Proposition: existence and uniqueness of the RSS minimizer.</summary>

::: {.proposition #prp-rss-min}
The residual sum of squares $\text{RSS}(\beta)$ in \@ref(eq:RSS) always attains a minimum. The minimizer is unique if and only if $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is invertible.
:::

*Proof.* We first establish that $\text{RSS}$ is a convex function with at least one critical point, which guarantees a global minimum. Expanding the quadratic form,

$$
\begin{equation}
\text{RSS}(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_i - x_{i}^{T}\beta)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_i^2 + (x_{i}^{T}\beta)^2 - 2y_ix_i^{T}\beta)
\end{equation}
$$

By linearity of summation and the identities $\sum_{i=1}^N x_ix_i^T= \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ and $\sum_{i=1}^N x_iy_i = \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}$, this becomes

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\text{RSS}(\beta) &= \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i^2 + \sum_{i=1}^{N}\beta^Tx_ix_i^T\beta - \sum_{i=1}^{N}2y_ix_i^{T}\beta\\
           &= \|\mathbf{y}\|^2 +\beta^T\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\beta - 2\beta^T\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

To establish convexity, we show that the Hessian $\nabla^2 \text{RSS}(\beta) = 2\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is positive semidefinite, noting that $\text{RSS}$ is twice differentiable. A matrix $M$ is positive semidefinite if $v^TMv \geq 0$ for all $v \in \mathbb{R}^p$. Since

$$
\begin{equation}
v^T\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}v = (\mathbf{X}v)^T\mathbf{X}v = \|\mathbf{X}v\|^2\geq0
\end{equation}
$$

it follows that $\text{RSS}$ is convex.

Next, we establish that a critical point exists and that it must be a minimum. To find a critical point, we compute the gradient[^1]:

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\nabla_{\beta}\text{RSS}(\beta) &= -2\mathbf{X}^T(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\beta) \\
                         &= -2\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} + 2\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\beta
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

Thus, a critical point must satisfy the normal equation $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\beta$. The problem of determining the existence of a critical point can now be reduced to a simple problem of determining that the normal equation is consistent:

A linear system $Ax = b$ has a solution if and only if $b \in \text{Col}(A)$. For the normal equations $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\beta = \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}$, we need $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} \in \text{Col}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})$. Since $\text{Col}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}) = \text{Col}(\mathbf{X}^T)$[^2] and $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}$ is, by definition, a linear combination of the columns of $\mathbf{X}^T$, we have $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} \in \text{Col}(\mathbf{X}^T) = \text{Col}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})$. Since a consistent system has at least one solution, RSS always has at least one critical point.

Lastly, we show that for a convex function any critical point is necessarily a global minimum. Let $f:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}$ be convex and differentiable, and suppose $\nabla f(x^*) = 0$. By the first-order characterization of convexity[^3]:

$$
\begin{equation}
f(x) \geq f(x^*) + \nabla f^T(x^*)(x-x^*) =  f(x^*) + 0(x-x^*) = f(x^*)
\end{equation}
$$

As $f(x) \geq f(x^*)$ for any $x,x^*\in \operatorname{dom}(f)$, $f(x^*)$ is a global minimum. Therefore a minimum always exists for the RSS.

However, this minimum is not necessarily unique. The uniqueness depends entirely on whether $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is invertible, leading to two cases:

Case 1: $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is invertible:

If the matrix $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is invertible, then:

$$
\begin{equation}
\hat\beta = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}
\end{equation}
$$

is the unique solution.

Case 2: $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is singular:

When $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is singular, $\text{Ker}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})$ is nontrivial. If $\beta_0$ is a solution to the normal equation and $\beta^*\in\text{Ker}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})$, such that $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\beta^* = 0$, then:

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}(\beta_0 + \beta^*) = \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\beta_0 + \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\beta^* = \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} + 0 = \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

Hence $\beta_0 + \beta^*$ is itself a solution, and the solution set is $\{\beta_0 + \beta^* \mid \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\beta_0 = \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y},\ \beta^*\in \text{Ker}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})\}$. Since $\text{Ker}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})$ is a nontrivial linear subspace and therefore has infinitely many elements[^4], the solution set forms an affine subspace with infinitely many elements.

Hence, while the minimum always exists, it is unique only when $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is invertible. $\qquad\square$
</details>

As shown previously, $\text{RSS}(\beta)$ can be written in matrix notation:

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\text{RSS}(\beta) &= \mathbf{y}^T\mathbf{y} +\beta^T\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\beta - 2\beta^T\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}\\
                  &= (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\beta)^T(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\beta)
\end{split}
(\#eq:RSSmatrix)
\end{equation}
$$

where $\mathbf{X}$ is an $N \times p$ matrix with each row an input vector, and $\mathbf{y}$ is an $N$-vector of the outputs in the training set. Differentiating with respect to $\beta$ we get the normal equations:

$$
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{X}^T(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\beta) = 0
(\#eq:normeq)
\end{equation}
$$
If $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is nonsingular, then we get the unique solution:

$$
\begin{equation}
\hat\beta = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}
(\#eq:normsol)
\end{equation}
$$

and the fitted value at the $i$th input $x_i$ is $\hat{y}_i = \hat{y}(x_i) = x^{T}_i\hat{\beta}$. At an arbitrary input $x_0$, the prediction is $\hat{y}(x_0) = x^{T}_0\hat{\beta}$. The entire fitted surface is characterized by the $p$ parameters $\hat{\beta}$.[^5] It seems that we may not need a very large data set to fit such a model.

### Linear Model Simulation

We simulate a data set with an output class variable $G$ with the values `r color("BLUE", "blue")` or `r color("ORANGE", "orange")`. There are 100 points in each of the two classes. We fit a linear regression model to these values, with the response $Y$ coded as $0$ for `r color("BLUE", "blue")` and $1$ for `r color("ORANGE", "orange")`. The fitted values $\hat{Y}$ are converted to a fitted class variable $\hat{G}$ according to the rule

$$
\begin{equation}
\hat{G} =
\begin{cases}
\text{ORANGE} & \hat{Y} > 0.5\\
\text{BLUE} & \hat{Y} \leq 0.5
\end{cases}
(\#eq:classlabel)
\end{equation}
$$

There are multiple scenarios where our constructed data can come from, but we outline here specifically two types:

**Scenario 1**: The training data in each class were generated from bivariate Gaussian distributions with uncorrelated components and different means.

In other words, our data is generated from each class $j$ with fixed mean $\mu^{(j)}$ and covariance $\Sigma^{(j)}$, and each observation $i$ is distributed with $X_i|Y=j \sim N(\mu^{(j)}, \Sigma^{(j)})$. Therefore, $\Pr(X|Y=j) = \phi(x;\mu^{(j)},\Sigma^{(j)})$.

**Scenario 2**: The training data in each class came from a mixture of 10 low-variance Gaussian distributions, with individual means themselves distributed as Gaussian.

Essentially, we have $10$ random cluster locations $\mu_k^{(j)}$ per class, each distributed around a class specific mean $\mu^{(j)}$ with covariance $\Sigma^{(j)}$. Then for each cluster location, we generate an observation $X_i$ where $X_i|\text{Location}=k,Y=j \sim N(\mu_k^{(j)}, \Sigma)$ where $\Sigma$ is the variance of the mixture distribution. Therefore, $\Pr(X|Y=j) = \sum_{k=1}^{10}\pi_k\phi(x;\mu_k^{(j)},\Sigma)$, where $\pi_k$ is the weight of the cluster (How likely/prominent this cluster is).

We first demonstrate the method of how our simulated data set is generated:

```{r, warning=FALSE}
# Generate data set of n=20 from two bivariate normal distribution
d1 <- mvrnorm(n = 10, c(1, 0), diag(2)) #BLUE
d2 <- mvrnorm(n = 10, c(0, 1), diag(2)) #ORANGE

gen_obs <- function(mean, nobs) {
  obs <- c()
  for (i in 1:nobs){
    row_mean <- mean[sample(1:10, 1), ]
    newobs <- mvrnorm(n = 1, row_mean, diag(1 / 5, 2, 2))
    obs <- rbind(obs, unname(newobs))
  }

  colnames(obs) <- c("x1", "x2")
  obs
}

d1_obs <- gen_obs(d1, 100)
d2_obs <- gen_obs(d2, 100)
Y <- rep(c(0, 1), each = 100) # 0=BLUE, 1=ORANGE
test_mat <- as.data.frame(cbind(Y, rbind(d1_obs, d2_obs)))
test_mat$Y <- factor(test_mat$Y, labels = c("Blue", "Orange"))

# Generate points grid
grid_size <- 100
x1_range <- range(test_mat$x1)
x2_range <- range(test_mat$x2)
grid_x1 <- seq(x1_range[1] - 1, x1_range[2] + 1, length.out = grid_size)
grid_x2 <- seq(x2_range[1] - 1, x2_range[2] + 1, length.out = grid_size)
grid_data <- expand.grid(x1 = grid_x1, x2 = grid_x2)
```

We generated $10$ centers $m_k^{(1)} \sim N((0,1)^T, I)$ for `r color("ORANGE", "orange")` class and $10$ centers $m_k^{(0)} \sim N((1,0)^T, I)$ for `r color("BLUE", "blue")` class. Then, to create a Gaussian mixture model, we select a mean $m_k$ from each class with probability $\pi_k = \frac{1}{10}$ and generate an observation from $N(m_k, I/5)$. We generate $100$ observations for each class using this method and train our model on the data.

```{r linearmodel, fig.cap="Classification example in two dimensions.", max_height = "50px", warning=FALSE}
# Fit simple linear model
lm_data <- data.frame(Y = as.numeric(test_mat$Y == "Orange"), x1 = test_mat$x1, x2 = test_mat$x2)
boundary_model <- lm(Y ~ x1 + x2, data = lm_data)

grid_predictions <- predict(boundary_model, grid_data)
grid_data$predicted_class <- ifelse(grid_predictions > 0.5, "Orange", "Blue")

# Create the plot with background
p <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = grid_data, aes(x = x1, y = x2, color = predicted_class),
             size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = test_mat, aes(x = x1, y = x2, color = Y),
             size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8, stroke = 1, shape = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#4A90E2", "#F5A623")) +
  labs(title = "Linear Regression") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "grey90", linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "dotted"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_line(color = "grey95", linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dotted"),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5),
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  ) +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 0.75)

# Add decision boundary line
boundary_slope <- -coef(boundary_model)[2] / coef(boundary_model)[3]
boundary_intercept <- (0.5 - coef(boundary_model)[1]) / coef(boundary_model)[3]

p + geom_abline(slope = boundary_slope, intercept = boundary_intercept,
                color = "black", linewidth = 1)
```

In \@ref(fig:linearmodel), the set of points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ classified as `r color("ORANGE", "orange")` corresponds to $\{x:x^T\hat{\beta} > 0.5\}$, and the two predicted classes are separated by the linear *decision boundary* $\{x:x^T\hat{\beta} = 0.5\}$. There are some misclassifications in the simulated data.

### Nearest-Neighbor Methods

The nearest-neighbor methods use observations in the training set $\mathcal{T}: \{(x_i, y_i),\;i=1,2,\ldots,N\}$ closest in input space to $x$ to obtain $\hat{Y}$. We define the $k$-nearest neighbor fit for $\hat{Y}$ as

$$
\hat{Y}(x) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{x_i\in N_k(x)} y_i
$$

where $N_k(x) = \{x_i \in \mathcal{T}:d(x_i,x) \leq d_{(k)}(x)\}$ is the $k$-nearest neighborhood of point $x$ and $|N_k| = k$. Here $d_{(k)}(x)$ denotes the $k$th smallest distance from $x$ to the training points, and $d(x_i,x)$ is the Euclidean norm $\|x_i-x\|_2$.[^6] The fitted value $\hat{Y}$ is converted to a class label $\hat{G}$ as in equation \@ref(eq:classlabel).

```{r KNNexample, echo=FALSE, fig.align="center", fig.cap="Example of a 3-NN algorithm."}
knitr::include_graphics("Chp2/pictures/note2_1.png")
```

We can further define $k$-NN more formally as:

Given a test point $\mathbf{x}$, define the neighborhood $N_k \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of its $k$ nearest neighbors, so that $|N_k| = k$ and, for every $(\mathbf{x}', y') \in \mathcal{T}\setminus N_k$,[^7]

$$
d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') \geq \max_{(\mathbf{x}'', y'') \in N_k} d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}'')
$$

We can now define a classifier $h$ as a function returning the most common label in $N_k$:

$$
h(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{mode}(\{y' : (\mathbf{x}', y') \in N_k\})
$$

where the neighborhood is classified by its most frequent label.

```{r knn1, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="The classes are fit by 15-nearest neighbor averaging. The predicted class is chosen by majority vote amongst the 15-nearest neighbors."}
train_features <- test_mat[, c("x1", "x2")]
test_data <- grid_data[, c("x1", "x2")]
train_labels <- test_mat$Y

# knn implementation
knn_model <- knn(train = train_features, test = test_data, cl = train_labels, k = 15)
grid_data$predicted_class <- knn_model
grid_data$pred_numeric <- as.numeric(knn_model == "Orange")

# Create the plot with background
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = grid_data, aes(x = x1, y = x2, color = predicted_class),
             size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_contour(data = grid_data, aes(x = x1, y = x2, z = pred_numeric),
               breaks = 0.5, size = 0.8, color = "black") +
  geom_point(data = test_mat, aes(x = x1, y = x2, color = Y),
             size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8, stroke = 1, shape = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#4A90E2", "#F5A623")) +
  labs(title = "15-Nearest Neighbor Classifier") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "grey90", linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "dotted"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_line(color = "grey95", linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dotted"),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5),
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  ) +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 0.75)
```

In Figure \@ref(fig:knn1), the same training data is used as in Figure \@ref(fig:linearmodel), and we used 15-nearest-neighbor averaging of the binary coded response as the method of fitting. $\hat{Y}$ is the proportion of `r color("ORANGE", "orange")`'s in the neighborhood, and so assigning class `r color("ORANGE", "orange")` to $\hat{G}$ if $\hat{Y} > 0.5$ is essentially a majority vote in the neighborhood. We see that the decision boundaries are irregular, non-linear, and respond to local clusters where one class dominates.

```{r knn2, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Classes are coded as a binary variable and then predicted by 1-nearest neighbor classification."}
# knn implementation
knn_model <- knn(train = train_features, test = grid_data[, c("x1", "x2")], cl = train_labels, k = 1)
grid_data$predicted_class <- knn_model
grid_data$pred_numeric <- as.numeric(knn_model == "Orange")

# Create the plot with background
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = grid_data, aes(x = x1, y = x2, color = predicted_class),
             size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_contour(data = grid_data, aes(x = x1, y = x2, z = pred_numeric),
               breaks = 0.5, size = 0.8, color = "black") +
  geom_point(data = test_mat, aes(x = x1, y = x2, color = Y),
             size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8, stroke = 1, shape = 1) +
  labs(title = "1-Nearest Neighbor Classifier") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#4A90E2", "#F5A623")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "grey90", linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "dotted"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_line(color = "grey95", linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dotted"),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5),
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  ) +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 0.75)
```

Figure \@ref(fig:knn2) instead shows the result for 1-nearest neighbor classification: $\hat{Y}$ is assigned the value $y_{\ell}$ of the closest point $x_{\ell}$ to $x$ in the training data. This corresponds to a Voronoi tessellation of the training data. Each point $x_i$ has an associated Voroni cell bounding the region where it is the only closest neighbor to any test point, such that, for all points $x$ in the cell, $\hat{G}(x) = g_i$. Compared to Figure \@ref(fig:knn1), the decision boundary is even more irregular. The training error is approximately an increasing function of $k$, and is always $0$ for $k=1$. As a consequence, we cannot use sum-of-squared errors on the training set as a criterion for picking $k$, as this would always result in picking $k=1$.

It appears that $k$-nearest neighbor fits have a single parameter, which is the number of neighbors $k$, compared to the $p$ parameters in least-squares fit. However, the effective number of parameters of $k$-NN is $N/k$, which is generally larger than $p$ and decreases with increasing $k$. Consider the hypothetical case where the neighborhoods are non-overlapping: given $N$ training points and $k$ points per neighborhood, we have $N/k$ neighborhoods. As a majority vote is cast for each neighborhood, this effectively constitutes one parameter per neighborhood.

```{r misclassification, warning=FALSE, fig.cap = "Misclassification curves. A single training sample of size 200 was used, and a test sample of size 10000. Orange curve is test and blue curve is training error for $k$-NN classification. Results for the linear regression are the orange and blue squares at 3 degrees of freedom."}
# Training set
train_obs1 <- gen_obs(d1, 5000)
train_obs2 <- gen_obs(d2, 5000)
Y <- rep(c(0, 1), each = 5000) # 0=BLUE, 1=ORANGE
train_mat <- as.data.frame(cbind(Y, rbind(train_obs1, train_obs2)))
train_mat$Y <- factor(train_mat$Y, labels = c("Blue", "Orange"))

# Test set
test_obs1 <- gen_obs(d1, 100)
test_obs2 <- gen_obs(d2, 100)
Y <- rep(c(0, 1), each = 100)
test_mat <- as.data.frame(cbind(Y, rbind(test_obs1, test_obs2)))
test_mat$Y <- factor(test_mat$Y, labels = c("Blue", "Orange"))

# KNN model
k <- c(1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 17, 21, 25, 31, 39, 45, 55, 69, 89, 101, 125, 151)
results <- data.frame(k = numeric(), test_error = numeric(), train_error = numeric())

for (kval in k){
  test_pred <- knn(train = train_mat[, c("x1", "x2")], test = test_mat[, c("x1", "x2")], cl = train_mat$Y, k = kval)
  train_pred <- knn(train = train_mat[, c("x1", "x2")], test = train_mat[, c("x1", "x2")], cl = train_mat$Y, k = kval)

  test_error <- mean(test_pred != test_mat$Y)
  train_error <- mean(train_pred != train_mat$Y)

  results <- rbind(results, data.frame(k = kval, test_error = test_error, train_error = train_error))
}

results$df <- 200 / results$k

# Linear
lm_data <- data.frame(Y = as.numeric(train_mat$Y == "Orange"), x1 = train_mat$x1, x2 = train_mat$x2)
lm_train <- lm(Y ~ x1 + x2, data = lm_data)

test_pred <- ifelse(predict(lm_train, test_mat[, c("x1", "x2")]) > 0.5, "Orange", "Blue")
train_pred <- ifelse(predict(lm_train, train_mat[, c("x1", "x2")]) > 0.5, "Orange", "Blue")

lm_test_error <- mean(test_pred != test_mat$Y)
lm_train_error <- mean(train_pred != train_mat$Y)
# bayes_error <- 0.21

ggplot(results, aes(x = df)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = train_error, color = "Train"), linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(y = train_error, color = "Train"), size = 2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = test_error, color = "Test"), linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "solid") +
  geom_point(aes(y = test_error, color = "Test"), size = 2) +
  # geom_hline(aes(yintercept = bayes_error, color = "Bayes"), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(x = 3, y = lm_train_error, color = "Train"), shape = 15, size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = 3, y = lm_test_error, color = "Test"), shape = 15, size = 2.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.5, y = lm_train_error + 0.01, label = "Linear", hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Train" = "#4A90E2", "Test" = "#F5A623", "Bayes" = "#8B4789"),
                     breaks = c("Train", "Test", "Bayes")) +
  scale_x_log10(
    name = "Degrees of Freedom = N/k",
    breaks = c(2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 18, 29, 67, 200),
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ 200 / ., name = "k = Number of Nearest Neighbors",
                        breaks = c(1, 3, 5, 7, 11, 21, 31, 45, 69, 101, 151))
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Test Error", limits = c(0, 0.35), breaks = seq(0.05, 0.3, 0.05)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = c(0.15, 0.15),
    legend.title = element_blank(),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.title.x.top = element_text(margin = margin(b = 10)),
    axis.title.x.bottom = element_text(margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 9),
    axis.ticks = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    axis.ticks.length = unit(0.2, "cm"),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5)
  )

```

## Statistical Decision Theory

We now develop a framework to evaluate the models discussed previously. Let $X \in \mathbb{R}^p$ denote a real-valued input vector, and $Y \in \mathbb{R}$ a real-valued random output variable, with joint distribution $\Pr(X,Y)$. We seek a function $f(X)$ for predicting $Y$ given input $X$. As we desire accurate models, we need a loss function $L(Y, f(X))$ that penalizes errors in prediction. The most common choice is the squared-error loss $L(Y, f(X)) = (Y - f(X))^2$, which gives us a criterion to select $f$.

### Regression Function

Given the squared error loss function, we now define the expected prediction error criterion:

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\text{EPE}(f) &= \mathbb{E}[(Y-f(X))^2] \\
       &= \int (y-f(x))^2\Pr(dx,dy)
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

By conditioning on $X$, we can write $\text{EPE}$ as:

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\text{EPE}(f) &= \int_{y\in Y}\int_{x\in X} (y-f(x))^2\;\Pr(X=x, Y=y)\;dx\;dy \\
              &= \int_{y\in Y}\int_{x\in X} (y-f(x))^2\;\Pr(Y=y\mid X=x)\;\Pr(X=x)\;dx\;dy \\
              &= \int_{x\in X}\left(\int_{y\in Y} (y-f(x))^2\;\Pr(Y=y\mid X=x)\;dy\right)\Pr(X=x)\;dx \\
              &= \mathbb{E}_X\,\mathbb{E}_{Y\mid X}[(Y - f(X))^2 \mid X]
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

We note that $\text{EPE}$ is an integral of the form:

$$
\begin{equation}
\text{EPE}(f) = \int_{x\in X} \mathbb{E}[(Y-f(x))^2\mid x]\; dx
\end{equation}
$$

Since the integrand is always non-negative and $f(x)$ can be chosen independently for each $x$, minimizing each integrand is equivalent to minimizing the integral. We therefore solve the simpler problem: at each point $x$, find a constant $c$ that minimizes $\mathbb{E}_{Y\mid X}[(Y-c)^2\mid X=x]$. In other words, it suffices to minimize $\text{EPE}$ pointwise.

<details>
<summary>Lemma: pointwise minimization of an integral functional.</summary>

::: {.lemma #lem-pointwise}
Let $(S, \mathcal{A}, \mu)$ be a measure space with $\mu$ a positive measure, let $\mathcal{H}$ be a space of measurable functions $f: S \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$, and let $F: \mathcal{H} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be the functional $F(f) = \int_{S} g(f(s),s) \, \mu(ds)$ for some measurable $g: \mathcal{X} \times S \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. If the pointwise minimizer $f^*(s) = \operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in\mathcal{X}} g(c,s)$ is measurable, then $f^*$ globally minimizes $F$ over $\mathcal{H}$.
:::

*Proof.* For any $f \in \mathcal{H}$, $g(f(s), s) \geq g(f^*(s), s)$ for every $s$ by the definition of $f^*$. Since $\mu$ is a positive measure, integration preserves the inequality:

$$
\begin{equation}
F(f) = \int_{S} g(f(s),s) \, \mu(ds) \geq \int_{S} g(f^*(s),s) \, \mu(ds) = F(f^*)
\end{equation}
$$

Hence $f^*$ is a global minimizer. The reduction relies on three conditions: the integrand at $s$ depends on $f$ only through $f(s)$; $\mu$ is a positive measure, so integration preserves inequalities; and the pointwise minimizer is measurable, ensuring $f^* \in \mathcal{H}$. $\qquad\square$
</details>

Applying Lemma \@ref(lem:lem-pointwise) with $g(c,x) = \mathbb{E}_{Y\mid X}[(Y-c)^2\mid X=x]$,

$$
\begin{equation}
f(x) = \operatorname*{argmin}_c \mathbb{E}_{Y\mid X}[(Y-c)^2\mid X=x]
\end{equation}
$$

To solve this optimization problem, we first expand the inner term:

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
f(x) &= \operatorname*{argmin}_c \mathbb{E}_{Y\mid X}[Y^2 - 2Yc + c^2\mid X=x] \\
     &= \operatorname*{argmin}_c \bigl(\mathbb{E}_{Y\mid X}[Y^2\mid X=x] - 2c\,\mathbb{E}_{Y\mid X}[Y\mid X=x] + c^2\bigr) \\
     &= \operatorname*{argmin}_c \bigl(c^2 - 2c\,\mathbb{E}_{Y\mid X}[Y\mid X=x] + \mathbb{E}_{Y\mid X}[Y^2\mid X=x]\bigr)
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

We take the derivative of the RHS with respect to $c$ and set it to $0$:

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
2c - 2\mathbb{E}_{Y\mid X}[Y\mid X=x] &= 0 \\
c &= \mathbb{E}_{Y\mid X}[Y\mid X=x]
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

Hence the solution to the optimization problem is the conditional expectation (regression function):

$$
\begin{equation}
f(x) = \mathbb{E}_{Y\mid X}[Y\mid X=x]
\end{equation}
$$

### Optimal Function of Nearest-Neighbor Method

For a fixed query point $x$, the $k$-NN estimator replaces the population objective $\mathbb{E}[(Y-c)^2 \mid X = x]$ with its empirical analog over the neighborhood $N_k(x)$:

$$
\begin{equation}
\hat{c} = \operatorname*{argmin}_c \sum_{x_i \in N_k(x)} (y_i - c)^2
\end{equation}
$$

Differentiating with respect to $c$ and setting to zero,

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\frac{d}{dc}\sum_{x_i \in N_k(x)}(y_i - c)^2 &= -2\sum_{x_i \in N_k(x)}(y_i - c) = 0 \\
\sum_{x_i \in N_k(x)} y_i &= \sum_{x_i \in N_k(x)} c \\
\hat{c} &= \frac{1}{k}\sum_{x_i \in N_k(x)} y_i = \operatorname{Ave}(y_i \mid x_i \in N_k(x))
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

The population conditional expectation $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x]$ is approximated in two steps: the sample average estimates $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X \in N_k(x)]$ by the law of large numbers as $k \to \infty$, and $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X \in N_k(x)] \to \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x]$ as the neighborhood shrinks when $k/N \to 0$.

### Optimal Function of Linear Model

Assuming that the regression function $f(x)$ is approximately linear:

$$
\begin{equation}
f(x) \approx x^{T}\beta
\end{equation}
$$

we plug this linear model into the $\text{EPE}$:

$$
\begin{equation}
\text{EPE}(f) = \mathbb{E}[(Y-f(X))^2] = \mathbb{E}[(Y-X^T\beta)^2]
\end{equation}
$$

Differentiating with respect to $\beta$ and interchanging the derivative and the integral (justified in the appendix to this chapter),

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\frac{\partial\text{EPE}(f)}{\partial \beta} &= \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta}(Y-X^T\beta)^2\right] \\
                                             &= \mathbb{E}[2(Y-X^T\beta)(-X)] \\
                                             &= -2\bigl(\mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[XX^T]\beta\bigr)
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

where the inner derivative uses the chain rule together with $\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta}(X^T\beta) = X$. Setting the gradient to zero,

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\mathbb{E}[XX^T]\beta &= \mathbb{E}[XY] \\
\beta &= (\mathbb{E}[XX^T])^{-1}\mathbb{E}[XY]
\end{split}
(\#eq:linearoptimal)
\end{equation}
$$

The least-squares solution approximates this theoretical $\beta$ when $N$ is large:

$$
\hat{\beta} = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} \xrightarrow{N\;\rightarrow\;\infty} (\mathbb{E}[XX^T])^{-1}\mathbb{E}[XY] = \beta
$$

<details>
<summary>Proposition: limit of the least-squares solution.</summary>

::: {.proposition #prp-lse-limit}
Under the linear model, the least-squares estimator converges to the population optimum \@ref(eq:linearoptimal) as the sample size grows:
$$
\hat{\beta} = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} \xrightarrow{N\to\infty} (\mathbb{E}[XX^T])^{-1}\mathbb{E}[XY] = \beta
$$
:::

*Proof.* Since $\mathbf{X}$ is the $N \times p$ matrix whose $i$th row is the observation $x_i^T$,

$$
\mathbf{X} =  \begin{bmatrix}x_1^T\\x_2^T\\\vdots\\x_N^T\end{bmatrix}
$$

By the law of large numbers applied to the i.i.d. observations,

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 & x_2 & \ldots & x_N \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_1^T\\x_2^T\\\vdots\\x_N^T\end{bmatrix}
                      &= \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_ix^T_i \approx N\,\mathbb{E}[XX^T]
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

and similarly, with $\mathbf{y}$ the $N$-vector of outputs,

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 & x_2 & \ldots & x_N \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}y_1\\y_2\\\vdots\\y_N\end{bmatrix}
                       &= \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_iy_i \approx N\,\mathbb{E}[XY]
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

Substituting both approximations, the factors of $N$ cancel:

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\hat{\beta} &= (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} \\
           &\approx (N\,\mathbb{E}[XX^T])^{-1}(N\,\mathbb{E}[XY]) \\
           &= (\mathbb{E}[XX^T])^{-1}\mathbb{E}[XY] = \beta
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

Thus the least-squares solution approaches the theoretical $\beta$ as $N$ grows. $\qquad\square$
</details>

### $L^1$ Loss

We show that under $L^1$ loss, $\text{EPE}(f)$ is minimized by $f(x) = \operatorname{median}(Y \mid X = x)$. We first recall that the median of any distribution is

$$
\begin{equation}
c^* = \inf\{t : F_X(t) \geq \tfrac{1}{2}\} = Q\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)
\end{equation}
$$

where $Q(p) := F_X^{-1}(p)$ is the quantile function.

We show that the median $c^*$ satisfies both:

$$
\begin{equation}
\text{(i)}\ \Pr(X \leq c^*) \geq \frac{1}{2} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \text{(ii)}\ \Pr(X \geq c^*) \geq \frac{1}{2}
\end{equation}
$$


To establish (i), take a sequence $\{t_n\}$ with $t_n \downarrow c^*$. Since each $t_n > c^* = \inf\{t : F_X(t) \geq 1/2\}$, each $t_n$ belongs to $\{t : F_X(t) \geq 1/2\}$, so $F_X(t_n) \geq 1/2$ for every $n$. By right-continuity of $F_X$, we have $F_X(t_n) \to F_X(c^*)$ as $t_n \downarrow c^*$, and hence $F_X(c^*) \geq 1/2$ and $\Pr(X \leq c^*) \geq 1/2$.

To establish (ii), let $t < c^*$. By definition of the infimum, $t \notin \{s : F_X(s) \geq 1/2\}$, so $F_X(t) < 1/2$. Taking $t \uparrow c^*$, we obtain $F_X(c^{*-}) \leq 1/2$. Since $F_X(c^{*-}) = \Pr(X < c^*)$, it follows that $\Pr(X < c^*) \leq 1/2$, and therefore:

$$
\begin{equation}
\Pr(X \geq c^*) = 1 - \Pr(X < c^*) \geq \frac{1}{2}
\end{equation}
$$

We now show that the median minimizes expected absolute deviation. Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable with $\mathbb{E}[|X|] < \infty$, and let $c^*$ be its median. Then for every $c \in \mathbb{R}$:

$$
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}[|X - c|] \geq \mathbb{E}[|X - c^*|]
\end{equation}
$$

We analyze three cases: (i) $c = c^*$, (ii) $c > c^*$, (iii) $c < c^*$.

(i) $c = c^*$, the inequality holds with equality.

(ii) Suppose that $c > c^*$, and let $\delta = c - c^* > 0$. We partition the real line into three events:

$$
\begin{equation}
A = \{X \leq c^*\}, \quad B = \{c^* < X \leq c\}, \quad C = \{X > c\}
\end{equation}
$$

We compute the pointwise difference $|X - c| - |X - c^*|$ on each event. On $A$, since $X \leq c^* < c$:

$$
\begin{equation}
|X - c| - |X - c^*| = (c - X) - (c^* - X) = c - c^* = \delta
\end{equation}
$$

On $B$, since $c^* < X \leq c$:

$$
\begin{equation}
|X - c| - |X - c^*| = (c - X) - (X - c^*) = c + c^* - 2X
\end{equation}
$$

On $C$, since $X > c > c^*$:

$$
\begin{equation}
|X - c| - |X - c^*| = (X - c) - (X - c^*) = -c + c^* = -\delta
\end{equation}
$$

Integrating over the partition:

$$
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}[|X - c|] - \mathbb{E}[|X - c^*|] = \delta \Pr(A) - \delta \Pr(C) + \mathbb{E}[(c + c^* - 2X)\mathbf{1}_B]
\end{equation}
$$

We simplify the $B$-term by writing $c + c^* - 2X = 2(c - X) - \delta$:

$$
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}[(c + c^* - 2X)\mathbf{1}_B] = 2\,\mathbb{E}[(c - X)\mathbf{1}_B] - \delta \Pr(B)
\end{equation}
$$

Substituting back and using $\Pr(A) + \Pr(B) + \Pr(C) = 1$ to write $\Pr(A) - \Pr(C) - \Pr(B) = 2\Pr(A) - 1$:

$$
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}[|X - c|] - \mathbb{E}[|X - c^*|] = \delta\bigl(2\Pr(X \leq c^*) - 1\bigr) + 2\,\mathbb{E}[(c - X)\mathbf{1}_B]
\end{equation}
$$

The first term is non-negative since $\delta > 0$ and $\Pr(X \leq c^*) \geq 1/2$ by (i). The second term is non-negative since on $B$ we have $X \leq c$, hence $c - X \geq 0$. Consequently $\mathbb{E}[|X - c|] \geq \mathbb{E}[|X - c^*|]$ for $c > c^*$.

(iii) Suppose that $c < c^*$, and let $\delta = c^* - c > 0$. We partition the real line into:

$$
\begin{equation}
A' = \{X < c\}, \quad B' = \{c \leq X < c^*\}, \quad C' = \{X \geq c^*\}
\end{equation}
$$

The same pointwise computation gives, on $A'$:

$$
\begin{equation}
|X - c| - |X - c^*| = (c - X) - (c^* - X) = c - c^* = -\delta
\end{equation}
$$

on $B'$:

$$
\begin{equation}
|X - c| - |X - c^*| = (X - c) - (c^* - X) = 2X - c - c^*
\end{equation}
$$

and on $C'$:

$$
\begin{equation}
|X - c| - |X - c^*| = (X - c) - (X - c^*) = c^* - c = \delta
\end{equation}
$$

Integrating and simplifying the $B'$-term by writing $2X - c - c^* = 2(X - c) - \delta$:

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\mathbb{E}[|X - c|] - \mathbb{E}[|X - c^*|] &= -\delta \Pr(A') + \delta \Pr(C') + 2\,\mathbb{E}[(X-c)\mathbf{1}_{B'}] - \delta \Pr(B') \\
&= \delta\bigl(2\Pr(X \geq c^*) - 1\bigr) + 2\,\mathbb{E}[(X - c)\mathbf{1}_{B'}]
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

where we used $\Pr(C') - \Pr(A') - \Pr(B') = 2\Pr(C') - 1$. The first term is non-negative by (ii), and the second is non-negative since $X \geq c$ on $B'$. Hence $\mathbb{E}[|X - c|] \geq \mathbb{E}[|X - c^*|]$ for $c < c^*$.

In all three cases the inequality holds.

Therefore under $L^1$ loss, the function $f^*(x) = \operatorname{median}(Y \mid X = x)$ minimizes the expected prediction error $\text{EPE}(f) = \mathbb{E}[|Y - f(X)|]$.

Given $\text{EPE}(f) = \mathbb{E}[|Y - f(X)|]$, we condition on $X$ and minimize pointwise:

$$
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}[|Y - f(X)|] = \mathbb{E}_X\,\mathbb{E}_{Y\mid X}[|Y - c| \mid X = x] \qquad c = f(x)
\end{equation}
$$

Hence:

$$
\begin{equation}
f(x) = \operatorname*{argmin}_c\, \mathbb{E}_{Y\mid X}[|Y - c| \mid X = x]
\end{equation}
$$

As we have established $\mathbb{E}[|X - c|] \geq \mathbb{E}[|X - c^*|]$ for every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the constant $c^*$ is the global minimizer. Hence $f(x) = \operatorname{median}(Y \mid X = x)$ is the solution.

### Optimal Function of Categorical Variable

When the output is a categorical variable $G$, a different loss function is needed. Let $\hat{G}$ be an estimate taking values in $\mathcal{G}$, the set of all possible classes. Our loss function can be represented as a $K \times K$ matrix $\mathbf{L}$, where $K = \text{card}(\mathcal{G})$. $\mathbf{L}$ will be zero on the diagonal and nonnegative elsewhere, where $L(k, \ell)$ is the loss for classifying an observation belonging to $\mathcal{G}_k$ as $\mathcal{G}_\ell$, i.e.

$$
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{L} = \begin{bmatrix}
              0 & L(\mathcal{G}_1, \mathcal{G}_2) & L(\mathcal{G}_1, \mathcal{G}_3) & \ldots  &L(\mathcal{G}_1, \mathcal{G}_K) \\
              L(\mathcal{G}_2, \mathcal{G}_1) & 0 & L(\mathcal{G}_2, \mathcal{G}_3) & \ldots  &L(\mathcal{G}_2, \mathcal{G}_K) \\
              \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
              L(\mathcal{G}_K, \mathcal{G}_1) & L(\mathcal{G}_K, \mathcal{G}_2) & L(\mathcal{G}_K, \mathcal{G}_3) & \ldots  &0
\end{bmatrix}
(\#eq:Lmatrix)
\end{equation}
$$

We use the zero-one loss, where every misclassification is penalized by a single unit:

$$
L(k, \ell) =
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } k=\ell \\
1 & \text{if } k \neq \ell
\end{cases}
$$

With respect to the joint distribution $\Pr(G, X)$, the expected prediction error is

$$
\text{EPE} = \mathbb{E}[L(G, \hat{G}(X))]
$$

Conditioning on $X$, we write the $\text{EPE}$ as

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\text{EPE} &= \mathbb{E}_X\,\mathbb{E}_{G\mid X}[L(G,\hat{G}(X)) \mid X] \\
           &= \mathbb{E}_X\!\left[\sum_{k=1}^{K} L(\mathcal{G}_k, \hat{G}(X))\,\Pr(\mathcal{G}_k \mid X)\right]
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

Minimizing pointwise,

$$
\hat{G}(x) = \operatorname*{argmin}_{g\in \mathcal{G}} \sum_{k=1}^{K} L(\mathcal{G}_k, g)\;\Pr(\mathcal{G}_k \mid X=x)
$$

Under zero-one loss the summand simplifies, since

$$
\begin{equation}
L(\mathcal{G}_k, g) =
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } \mathcal{G}_k = g \\
1 & \text{if } \mathcal{G}_k \neq g
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
$$

so only the terms with $\mathcal{G}_k \neq g$ survive:

$$
\hat{G}(x) = \operatorname*{argmin}_{g\in\mathcal{G}} \sum_{k:\mathcal{G}_k \neq g} \Pr(\mathcal{G}_k \mid X=x)
$$

Since $\Pr(\mathcal{G}_k \mid X=x)$ sums to one over $k$, and each class either equals $g$ or does not,

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\sum_{k=1}^{K}  \Pr(\mathcal{G}_k \mid X=x) &= 1 \\
\Pr(g \mid X=x) + \sum_{k:\mathcal{G}_k \neq g}  \Pr(\mathcal{G}_k \mid X=x) &= 1 \\
\sum_{k:\mathcal{G}_k \neq g}\Pr(\mathcal{G}_k \mid X=x) &= 1 - \Pr(g \mid X=x)
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

Substituting, the minimizer becomes

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\hat{G}(x) = \operatorname*{argmin}_{g\in\mathcal{G}} \sum_{k:\mathcal{G}_k \neq g} \Pr(\mathcal{G}_k \mid X=x) &= \operatorname*{argmin}_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\bigl(1-\Pr(g \mid X=x)\bigr) \\ &= \operatorname*{argmax}_{g\in\mathcal{G}} \Pr(g \mid X=x)
\end{split}
(\#eq:Bclass)
\end{equation}
$$

The solution is known as a *Bayes classifier*: it classifies each point to the most probable class under the conditional distribution $\Pr(G \mid X)$.

```{r bayes, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Optimal Bayes decision boundary"}
compute_mixture_density <- function(x, centers, var) {
  n_components <- nrow(centers)
  density <- 0
  for (i in 1:n_components){
    density <- density + dmvnorm(x, centers[i, ], sigma = diag(var, 2))
  }

  density / n_components
}

grid_data$prob_blue <- apply(grid_data[, c("x1", "x2")], 1, function(x) compute_mixture_density(x, d1, 1 / 5))
grid_data$prob_orange <- apply(grid_data[, c("x1", "x2")], 1, function(x) compute_mixture_density(x, d2, 1 / 5))

grid_data$predicted_class <- ifelse(grid_data$prob_orange > grid_data$prob_blue, "Orange", "Blue")
grid_data$pred_numeric <- as.numeric(grid_data$predicted_class == "Orange")

# Plot
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = grid_data, aes(x = x1, y = x2, color = predicted_class),
             size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_contour(data = grid_data, aes(x = x1, y = x2, z = pred_numeric),
               breaks = 0.5, size = 0.8, color = "black") +
  geom_point(data = test_mat, aes(x = x1, y = x2, color = Y),
             size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8, stroke = 1, shape = 1) +
  labs(title = "Bayes Optimal Classifier") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#4A90E2", "#F5A623")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "grey90", linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "dotted"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_line(color = "grey95", linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dotted"),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5),
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  ) +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 0.75)
```

$k$-nearest neighbor approximates the Bayes solution — except that the conditional probability at a point is relaxed to the conditional probability within a neighborhood of that point.

## Local Methods in High Dimensions

### Neighborhoods in $n$-Dimensional Volume

Our intuition suggests that, given a sufficiently large training set, we could always approximate the theoretically optimal conditional expectation through $k$-nearest neighbor averaging — since we should be able to find a large neighborhood of observations close to $x$ and average over them. This intuition, however, breaks down in high dimensions.

Consider the $p$-dimensional unit hypercube. Suppose we grow a hypercubical neighborhood around a target point to capture a fraction $r$ of the observations. Since this corresponds to a fraction $r$ of the unit volume, the expected edge length is $e_p(r) = r^{1/p}$. As the dimension increases, the expected edge length grows, so the neighborhood can no longer be considered "local". Reducing $r$ does not help, since the fewer observations we average, the higher the variance becomes.

```{r volume, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Curse of dimensionality illustrated. 80% of the range of each coordinate will be needed to capture 10% of the data in a 10-dimensional hypercube."}
r <- seq(0, 0.65, length.out = 500)
dims <- c(1, 2, 3, 10)
df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(dims, function(p) {
  data.frame(r = r, distance = r^(1 / p), p = factor(paste0("p=", p)))
}))

ggplot(df, aes(x = r, y = distance, color = p)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.1, 0.3), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey0", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.65), breaks = seq(0, 0.6, by = 0.2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    x = "Fraction of Volume",
    y = "Distance"
  )
```

### Median Distance to the Nearest Neighbor

Another consequence is that sample points are close to an edge of the sample. Consider $N$ data points uniformly distributed in a $p$-dimensional ball centered at the origin. Suppose we consider a nearest-neighbor estimate at the origin. The median distance from the origin to the closest data point is:

$$
\begin{equation}
d(p, N) = \left(1 - \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{1/N}\right)^{1/p}
(\#eq:mediandist)
\end{equation}
$$

<details>
<summary>Proof of median nearest-neighbor distance formula.</summary>

The proof proceeds in three stages: computation of the Jacobian determinant of the $p$-dimensional spherical coordinate map by induction; derivation of the volume of the $p$-ball via the reduction formula for $I_n = \int_0^\pi \sin^n\theta\,d\theta$ and a telescoping product of Gamma values; and finally, the order-statistic argument yielding the median.

::: {.lemma}
Define the $p$-dimensional spherical coordinate map $\Phi_p : (r, \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{p-1}) \mapsto (x_1, \ldots, x_p)$ by

$$
\begin{equation}
x_j = r\!\left(\prod_{k=1}^{j-1}\sin\theta_k\right)\cos\theta_j, \quad j = 1,\ldots,p-1,
\qquad
x_p = r\prod_{k=1}^{p-1}\sin\theta_k
(\#eq:sphericalmap)
\end{equation}
$$

where $\theta_k \in [0,\pi]$ for $k = 1,\ldots,p-2$, $\theta_{p-1} \in [0,2\pi)$, and empty products equal one. Then the Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{equation}
J_p := \left|\det D\Phi_p\right| = r^{p-1}\prod_{k=1}^{p-2}\sin^{p-1-k}\theta_k
(\#eq:jacobian)
\end{equation}
$$
:::

*Proof.* The proof is by induction on $p$. The coordinate formulas satisfy the recursion

$$
\begin{equation}
\Phi_p(r,\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_{p-1}) = \bigl(r\cos\theta_1,\;\sin\theta_1\cdot\Phi_{p-1}(r,\theta_2,\ldots,\theta_{p-1})\bigr)
(\#eq:phirecursion)
\end{equation}
$$

which is verified directly: the first coordinate is $r\cos\theta_1$, and for $j \geq 2$,

$$
x_j = r\!\left(\prod_{k=1}^{j-1}\sin\theta_k\right)\cos\theta_j = r\sin\theta_1\!\left(\prod_{k=2}^{j-1}\sin\theta_k\right)\cos\theta_j = \sin\theta_1\cdot[\Phi_{p-1}(r,\theta_2,\ldots)]_j
$$

confirming that $(x_2,\ldots,x_p) = \sin\theta_1\cdot\Phi_{p-1}(r,\theta_2,\ldots,\theta_{p-1})$.

For the base case $p = 2$, the map is $(r,\theta_1)\mapsto(r\cos\theta_1, r\sin\theta_1)$ and its Jacobian determinant is

$$
\det D\Phi_2 = \det\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta_1 & -r\sin\theta_1 \\ \sin\theta_1 & r\cos\theta_1\end{pmatrix} = r\cos^2\theta_1 + r\sin^2\theta_1 = r
$$

confirming $J_2 = r$ with the empty product equal to one.

Assume inductively that $J_{p-1} = r^{p-2}\prod_{k=1}^{p-3}\sin^{p-2-k}\theta_{k+1}$, where angles are indexed from $\theta_2$. Differentiating the recursion \@ref(eq:phirecursion), the Jacobian matrix $D\Phi_p$ takes the block form

$$
D\Phi_p = \begin{pmatrix}
\cos\theta_1 & -r\sin\theta_1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\[4pt]
\sin\theta_1\,\partial_r\Phi_{p-1} &
\cos\theta_1\,\Phi_{p-1} &
\sin\theta_1\,\partial_{\theta_2}\Phi_{p-1} &
\cdots &
\sin\theta_1\,\partial_{\theta_{p-1}}\Phi_{p-1}
\end{pmatrix}
$$

where $\partial_r\Phi_{p-1}$, $\Phi_{p-1}$, and each $\partial_{\theta_k}\Phi_{p-1}$ are $(p-1)$-dimensional column vectors occupying rows 2 through $p$. Expanding the determinant along the first row,

$$
\det(D\Phi_p) = \cos\theta_1\cdot M_{11} + (-r\sin\theta_1)\cdot(-1)^{1+2}\cdot M_{12} = \cos\theta_1\cdot M_{11} + r\sin\theta_1\cdot M_{12}
$$

where $M_{11}$ and $M_{12}$ are the corresponding unsigned minors.

In $M_{11}$, column 1 is $\cos\theta_1\,\Phi_{p-1}$ and columns $2$ through $p-1$ are $\sin\theta_1\,\partial_{\theta_k}\Phi_{p-1}$ for $k = 2,\ldots,p-1$. Factoring $\cos\theta_1$ from the first column and $\sin\theta_1$ from each of the remaining $p-2$ columns,

$$
M_{11} = \cos\theta_1\sin^{p-2}\theta_1\cdot\det\!\bigl[\Phi_{p-1}\mid\partial_{\theta_2}\Phi_{p-1}\mid\cdots\mid\partial_{\theta_{p-1}}\Phi_{p-1}\bigr]
$$

Since every component of $\Phi_{p-1}$ is linear in $r$, the map is homogeneous of degree one, giving $\Phi_{p-1}(r,\cdot) = r\,\partial_r\Phi_{p-1}(r,\cdot)$. Replacing the first column $\Phi_{p-1}$ by $r\,\partial_r\Phi_{p-1}$ and factoring $r$ out of that column,

$$
\det\!\bigl[\Phi_{p-1}\mid\partial_{\theta_2}\Phi_{p-1}\mid\cdots\bigr] = r\cdot\det\!\bigl[\partial_r\Phi_{p-1}\mid\partial_{\theta_2}\Phi_{p-1}\mid\cdots\bigr] = r\,J_{p-1}
$$

and hence $M_{11} = r\cos\theta_1\sin^{p-2}\theta_1\,J_{p-1}$.

In $M_{12}$, every column carries a factor of $\sin\theta_1$: column 1 is $\sin\theta_1\,\partial_r\Phi_{p-1}$ and the remaining $p-2$ columns are $\sin\theta_1\,\partial_{\theta_k}\Phi_{p-1}$. Factoring $\sin\theta_1$ from all $p-1$ columns,

$$
M_{12} = \sin^{p-1}\theta_1\cdot\det\!\bigl[\partial_r\Phi_{p-1}\mid\partial_{\theta_2}\Phi_{p-1}\mid\cdots\bigr] = \sin^{p-1}\theta_1\,J_{p-1}
$$

Substituting both minors into the expansion and collecting,

$$
\det(D\Phi_p) = r\cos^2\theta_1\sin^{p-2}\theta_1\,J_{p-1} + r\sin^p\theta_1\,J_{p-1} = r\,J_{p-1}\sin^{p-2}\theta_1\underbrace{\bigl(\cos^2\theta_1 + \sin^2\theta_1\bigr)}_{=\,1} = r\sin^{p-2}\theta_1\,J_{p-1}
$$

Applying the inductive hypothesis and re-indexing the product via $m = k+1$,

$$
J_p = r\sin^{p-2}\theta_1\cdot r^{p-2}\prod_{k=1}^{p-3}\sin^{p-2-k}\theta_{k+1} = r^{p-1}\sin^{p-2}\theta_1\prod_{m=2}^{p-2}\sin^{p-1-m}\theta_m = r^{p-1}\prod_{k=1}^{p-2}\sin^{p-1-k}\theta_k
$$

where the $k=1$ term of the final product recovers $\sin^{p-2}\theta_1$, completing the induction. $\qquad\square$

---

::: {.proposition}
The volume of the $p$-dimensional ball of radius $R$ is

$$
\begin{equation}
V_p(R) = \frac{\pi^{p/2}}{\Gamma\!\left(\frac{p}{2}+1\right)}R^p
(\#eq:volball)
\end{equation}
$$
:::

*Proof.* By the Lemma, the volume element is $r^{p-1}\prod_{k=1}^{p-2}\sin^{p-1-k}\theta_k\,dr\,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_{p-1}$. Since the integrand separates over independent variables,

$$
\begin{equation}
V_p(R) = \underbrace{\int_0^R r^{p-1}\,dr}_{=\,R^p/p} \cdot \underbrace{\int_0^{2\pi}d\theta_{p-1}}_{=\,2\pi} \cdot \prod_{k=1}^{p-2}\underbrace{\int_0^\pi\sin^{p-1-k}\theta_k\,d\theta_k}_{=\,I_{p-1-k}}
\end{equation}
$$

where $I_n := \int_0^\pi\sin^n\theta\,d\theta$. Re-indexing via $j = p-1-k$ (as $k$ runs from $1$ to $p-2$, $j$ runs over the same set $\{1,\ldots,p-2\}$),

$$
\begin{equation}
V_p(R) = \frac{R^p}{p}\cdot 2\pi\cdot\prod_{j=1}^{p-2}I_j
(\#eq:volprod)
\end{equation}
$$

Integrating by parts with $u = \sin^{n-1}\theta$ and $dv = \sin\theta\,d\theta$, so $du = (n-1)\sin^{n-2}\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta$ and $v = -\cos\theta$,

$$
I_n = \bigl[-\sin^{n-1}\theta\cos\theta\bigr]_0^\pi + (n-1)\int_0^\pi\sin^{n-2}\theta\cos^2\theta\,d\theta
$$

Since $\sin(0) = \sin(\pi) = 0$, the boundary term vanishes. Substituting $\cos^2\theta = 1-\sin^2\theta$ and splitting,

$$
I_n = (n-1)\int_0^\pi\sin^{n-2}\theta\,d\theta - (n-1)\int_0^\pi\sin^n\theta\,d\theta = (n-1)I_{n-2} - (n-1)I_n
$$

Adding $(n-1)I_n$ to both sides and dividing by $n$,

$$
\begin{equation}
I_n = \frac{n-1}{n}\,I_{n-2}
(\#eq:Inreduction)
\end{equation}
$$

with base cases $I_0 = \pi$ and $I_1 = 2$.

For even $n = 2m$ with $m \geq 1$, applying \@ref(eq:Inreduction) repeatedly until reaching $I_0$,

$$
\begin{equation}
I_{2m} = \frac{2m-1}{2m}\cdot\frac{2m-3}{2m-2}\cdots\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\cdot I_0 = \frac{(2m-1)!!}{(2m)!!}\,\pi
(\#eq:Ieven)
\end{equation}
$$

For odd $n = 2m+1$ with $m \geq 0$, applying \@ref(eq:Inreduction) repeatedly until reaching $I_1$,

$$
\begin{equation}
I_{2m+1} = \frac{2m}{2m+1}\cdot\frac{2m-2}{2m-1}\cdots\frac{4}{5}\cdot\frac{2}{3}\cdot I_1 = \frac{(2m)!!}{(2m+1)!!}\cdot 2
(\#eq:Iodd)
\end{equation}
$$

Using the double factorial identities $(2m)!! = 2^m m!$ and $(2m-1)!! = 2^m\Gamma(m+\tfrac{1}{2})/\sqrt{\pi}$, we substitute into \@ref(eq:Ieven) for the even case:

$$
I_{2m} = \frac{\dfrac{2^m\,\Gamma(m+\frac{1}{2})}{\sqrt{\pi}}}{2^m m!}\,\pi = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma\!\left(m+\tfrac{1}{2}\right)}{m!} = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma\!\left(m+\tfrac{1}{2}\right)}{\Gamma(m+1)}
$$

Setting $n = 2m$, so $m = n/2$, gives $I_n = \sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma\!\bigl(\tfrac{n+1}{2}\bigr)/\Gamma\!\bigl(\tfrac{n}{2}+1\bigr)$.

For the odd case, the functional equation $\Gamma(m+\tfrac{3}{2}) = (m+\tfrac{1}{2})\Gamma(m+\tfrac{1}{2})$ applied recursively gives $(2m+1)!! = 2^{m+1}\Gamma(m+\tfrac{3}{2})/\sqrt{\pi}$. Substituting into \@ref(eq:Iodd),

$$
I_{2m+1} = \frac{2^m m!}{\dfrac{2^{m+1}\Gamma(m+\frac{3}{2})}{\sqrt{\pi}}}\cdot 2 = \frac{2^{m+1}m!\sqrt{\pi}}{2^{m+1}\Gamma\!\left(m+\tfrac{3}{2}\right)} = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma(m+1)}{\Gamma\!\left(m+\tfrac{3}{2}\right)}
$$

Setting $n = 2m+1$, so $\Gamma(m+1) = \Gamma\!\bigl(\tfrac{n+1}{2}\bigr)$ and $\Gamma(m+\tfrac{3}{2}) = \Gamma\!\bigl(\tfrac{n}{2}+1\bigr)$, gives the same expression. Both parities therefore yield the unified form

$$
\begin{equation}
I_n = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{n+1}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{n}{2}+1\right)}
(\#eq:Ingamma)
\end{equation}
$$

Substituting $I_n$ into the product in \@ref(eq:volprod), and writing $\sqrt{\pi} = \Gamma\!\bigl(\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr)$ and using the identity $\Gamma\!\bigl(\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr)^{p-2} = \pi^{(p-2)/2}$,

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\prod_{j=1}^{p-2}I_j = \prod_{j=1}^{p-2}\frac{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{j+1}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{j+2}{2}\right)}
                     = \pi^{(p-2)/2}\prod_{j=1}^{p-2}\frac{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{j+1}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{j+2}{2}\right)}
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

Writing the product explicitly,

$$
\prod_{j=1}^{p-2}\frac{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{j+1}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{j+2}{2}\right)} = \frac{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{2}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{3}{2}\right)}\cdot\frac{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{3}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{4}{2}\right)}\cdot\frac{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{4}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{5}{2}\right)}\cdots\frac{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{p-1}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{p}{2}\right)}
$$

all interior terms cancel telescopically, leaving

$$
\frac{\Gamma(1)}{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{p}{2}\right)} = \frac{1}{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{p}{2}\right)}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{equation}
\prod_{j=1}^{p-2}I_j = \frac{\pi^{(p-2)/2}}{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{p}{2}\right)}
(\#eq:prodIj)
\end{equation}
$$

Substituting \@ref(eq:prodIj) into \@ref(eq:volprod),

$$
V_p(R) = \frac{R^p}{p}\cdot 2\pi\cdot\frac{\pi^{(p-2)/2}}{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{p}{2}\right)} = \frac{2\pi^{p/2}R^p}{p\,\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{p}{2}\right)}
$$

Applying $\Gamma\!\bigl(\tfrac{p}{2}+1\bigr) = \tfrac{p}{2}\,\Gamma\!\bigl(\tfrac{p}{2}\bigr)$, so that $p\,\Gamma\!\bigl(\tfrac{p}{2}\bigr) = 2\,\Gamma\!\bigl(\tfrac{p}{2}+1\bigr)$

$$
V_p(R) = \frac{2\pi^{p/2}R^p}{2\,\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{p}{2}+1\right)} = \frac{\pi^{p/2}}{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{p}{2}+1\right)}R^p \qquad\square
$$

---

*Proof.* Since $X_1$ is uniformly distributed on $\mathbb{B}^p$, the probability that $X_1$ lies within distance $m$ of the origin is the ratio of volumes. By the Proposition, the normalization constants cancel:

$$
\Pr(\|X_1\|\leq m) = \frac{V_p(m)}{V_p(1)} = \frac{\dfrac{\pi^{p/2}}{\Gamma(p/2+1)}\,m^p}{\dfrac{\pi^{p/2}}{\Gamma(p/2+1)}} = m^p
$$

Thus the CDF of $\|X_1\|$ is $F(m) = m^p$. Let $D_{(1)} = \min_{i=1}^{N}\|X_i\|$. The event $\{D_{(1)} > m\}$ is the intersection of $N$ independent events, each with probability $1-m^p$, so

$$
\Pr(D_{(1)} > m) = \prod_{i=1}^{N}\Pr(\|X_i\| > m) = (1-m^p)^N
$$

and therefore $\Pr(D_{(1)}\leq m) = 1-(1-m^p)^N$. The median $d = d(p,N)$ satisfies $\Pr(D_{(1)}\leq d) = \tfrac{1}{2}$, giving

$$
1-(1-d^p)^N = \tfrac{1}{2} \implies (1-d^p)^N = \tfrac{1}{2} \implies 1-d^p = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{1/N} \implies d(p,N) = \left(1-\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{1/N}\right)^{1/p}
$$

</details>

For $p = 10$ and $N = 500$, this gives $d(10,500) \approx 0.52$, meaning the nearest neighbor is typically more than halfway to the boundary. Thus the nearest neighbor of the origin is not at all local, and this effect worsens rapidly with dimension.

### Mean Squared Error Decomposition

Let $\hat{y}_0$ be any estimator of $f(x_0)$ trained on a random training set $\mathcal{T}$. The mean squared error at a fixed test point $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^p$ is

$$
\begin{equation}
\text{MSE}(x_0) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}\bigl[f(x_0) - \hat{y}_0\bigr]^2
(\#eq:mse)
\end{equation}
$$

This decomposes into a variance and a squared-bias term:

$$
\begin{equation}
\text{MSE}(x_0) = \text{Var}_{\mathcal{T}}(\hat{y}_0) + \text{Bias}^2(\hat{y}_0)
(\#eq:mse-decomp)
\end{equation}
$$

where $\text{Bias}(\hat{y}_0) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[\hat{y}_0] - f(x_0)$.

<details>
<summary>Proof of the bias-variance decomposition</summary>

*Proof.* Set $b = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[\hat{y}_0]$, a constant with respect to $\mathcal{T}$. Write $f(x_0) - \hat{y}_0 = (f(x_0) - b) + (b - \hat{y}_0)$ and expand the square:

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\text{MSE}(x_0) &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}\bigl[(f(x_0) - b)^2 + (b - \hat{y}_0)^2 + 2(f(x_0) - b)(b - \hat{y}_0)\bigr] \\
                &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}\bigl[(b - \hat{y}_0)^2\bigr] + (f(x_0) - b)^2 + 2(f(x_0) - b)\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}\bigl[b - \hat{y}_0\bigr]
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

The cross term vanishes: $\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[b - \hat{y}_0] = b - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[\hat{y}_0] = 0$ by the definition of $b$. The first term is $\text{Var}_{\mathcal{T}}(\hat{y}_0)$ and the second is $\text{Bias}^2(\hat{y}_0) = (f(x_0) - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[\hat{y}_0])^2$, giving

$$
\text{MSE}(x_0) = \text{Var}_{\mathcal{T}}(\hat{y}_0) + \text{Bias}^2(\hat{y}_0) \qquad\square
$$
</details>

### EPE of the Least-Squares Estimator

We now derive the EPE of the least-squares estimator $\hat{y}_0 = x_0^T\hat{\beta}$ under the model $y = X^T\beta + \varepsilon$ where $\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$ is independent of $X$. Since the test output $y_0 = x_0^T\beta + \varepsilon_0$ is itself random, the appropriate criterion integrates over both the test output and the random training set:

$$
\begin{equation}
\text{EPE}(x_0) = \mathbb{E}_{y_0 \mid x_0}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}\bigl[(y_0 - \hat{y}_0)^2\bigr]
(\#eq:epe-noisy)
\end{equation}
$$

where $\hat{\beta} = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}$. Since the least-squares estimator is unbiased under correct specification, the bias term in \@ref(eq:mse-decomp) vanishes, and the EPE becomes

$$
\begin{equation}
\text{EPE}(x_0) = \sigma^2 + \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}\bigl[x_0^T(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}x_0\bigr]\,\sigma^2
(\#eq:epe-linear)
\end{equation}
$$

The first term $\sigma^2$ is the irreducible variance of $y_0$ itself; the second is the estimation variance of $\hat{y}_0$ induced by the randomness in $\mathcal{T}$.

<details>
<summary>Proof of EPE decomposition for a linear estimator</summary>

Four lemmas are established before the main argument.

::: {.lemma #lem-linear-rep}
**Linear representation of** $\hat{y}_0$**.** The prediction $\hat{y}_0$ satisfies

$$
\hat{y}_0 = x_0^T\beta + \sum_{i=1}^N l_i(x_0)\,\varepsilon_i
$$

where $l(x_0) = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^N$ and $l_i(x_0)$ is its $i$th component.
:::

*Proof.* Substituting $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\beta + \varepsilon$ into $\hat{y}_0 = x_0^T\hat{\beta}$:

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\hat{y}_0 &= x_0^T(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} \\
          &= x_0^T(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T(\mathbf{X}\beta + \varepsilon) \\
          &= x_0^T(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\beta + x_0^T(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\varepsilon \\
          &= x_0^T\beta + x_0^T(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\varepsilon
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

Setting $l(x_0)^T = x_0^T(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times N}$ gives $x_0^T(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\varepsilon = \sum_{i=1}^N l_i(x_0)\varepsilon_i$, whence the stated representation follows.

::: {.lemma #lem-unbiased}
**Unbiasedness.** The least-squares estimator satisfies $\mathbb{E}_\varepsilon[\hat{\beta} \mid \mathbf{X}] = \beta$ and $\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}] = \beta$.
:::

*Proof.* Conditioning on $\mathbf{X}$ and substituting $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\beta + \varepsilon$:

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\mathbb{E}_\varepsilon[\hat{\beta} \mid \mathbf{X}] &= (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbb{E}_\varepsilon[\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{X}] \\
                                                  &= (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbb{E}_\varepsilon[\mathbf{X}\beta + \varepsilon \mid \mathbf{X}] \\
                                                  &= (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\beta + (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid \mathbf{X}] \\
                                                  &= \beta + 0 = \beta
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

where the last equality uses $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid \mathbf{X}] = 0$ by assumption. Unconditional unbiasedness follows from the tower property: $\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}}[\mathbb{E}_\varepsilon[\hat{\beta} \mid \mathbf{X}]] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}}[\beta] = \beta$.

::: {.lemma #lem-cond-mean}
**Conditional mean of** $y_0$**.** The conditional expectation satisfies $\mathbb{E}[y_0 \mid x_0] = x_0^T\beta$.
:::

*Proof.* Writing $y_0 = x_0^T\beta + \varepsilon_0$ and applying linearity of conditional expectation:

$$
\mathbb{E}[y_0 \mid x_0] = \mathbb{E}[x_0^T\beta + \varepsilon_0 \mid x_0] = x_0^T\beta + \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_0 \mid x_0] = x_0^T\beta
$$

where $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_0 \mid x_0] = 0$ holds by assumption.

::: {.lemma #lem-var}
**Variance of** $\hat{y}_0$**.** The training-set variance of $\hat{y}_0$ satisfies

$$
\text{Var}_{\mathcal{T}}(\hat{y}_0) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}\bigl[x_0^T(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}x_0\bigr]\,\sigma^2
$$
:::

The proof relies on the following sub-lemma.

**Sub-lemma (Expectation of a quadratic form)**. For a fixed vector $z \in \mathbb{R}^p$ and a random matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}$,

$$
\mathbb{E}[z^TAz] = z^T\mathbb{E}[A]\,z
$$

*Proof.* Since $z$ is fixed, expanding the quadratic form and applying linearity of expectation:

$$
\mathbb{E}[z^TAz] = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^p\sum_{j=1}^p z_i A_{ij} z_j\right] = \sum_{i=1}^p\sum_{j=1}^p z_i\,\mathbb{E}[A_{ij}]\,z_j = z^T\mathbb{E}[A]\,z \qquad\square
$$

*Proof.* Since $\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[\hat{y}_0] = x_0^T\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[\hat{\beta}] = x_0^T\beta$ by Lemma \@ref(lem:lem-unbiased), we have $\hat{y}_0 - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[\hat{y}_0] = x_0^T\hat{\beta} - x_0^T\beta = x_0^T(\hat{\beta} - \beta)$. Thus

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\text{Var}_{\mathcal{T}}(\hat{y}_0) &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}\bigl[(\hat{y}_0 - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[\hat{y}_0])^2\bigr] \\
                                    &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}\bigl[x_0^T(\hat{\beta} - \beta)(\hat{\beta} - \beta)^Tx_0\bigr] \\
                                    &= x_0^T\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}\bigl[(\hat{\beta} - \beta)(\hat{\beta} - \beta)^T\bigr]\,x_0 \\
                                    &= x_0^T\,\text{Var}_{\mathcal{T}}(\hat{\beta})\,x_0
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

where the third line applies the sub-lemma with $z = x_0$ and $A = (\hat{\beta} - \beta)(\hat{\beta} - \beta)^T$, and the last uses $\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{T}[\hat{\beta}] = \beta$ from Lemma \@ref(lem:lem-unbiased). It remains to compute $\text{Var}_{\mathcal{T}}(\hat{\beta})$. By the law of total variance over $(\mathbf{X}, \varepsilon)$:

$$
\text{Var}_{\mathcal{T}}(\hat{\beta}) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}}\bigl[\text{Var}_\varepsilon(\hat{\beta} \mid \mathbf{X})\bigr] + \text{Var}_{\mathbf{X}}\bigl[\mathbb{E}_\varepsilon[\hat{\beta} \mid \mathbf{X}]\bigr]
$$

The second term is $\text{Var}_{\mathbf{X}}[\beta] = 0$ since $\beta$ is a fixed constant. For the first term, since $\hat{\beta} = \beta + (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\varepsilon$ and $\beta$ is a constant:

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\text{Var}_\varepsilon(\hat{\beta} \mid \mathbf{X}) &= \text{Var}_\varepsilon\bigl((\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\varepsilon \mid \mathbf{X}\bigr) \\
                                                    &= (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\,\text{Var}(\varepsilon \mid \mathbf{X})\,\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1} \\
                                                    &= (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T(\sigma^2 I)\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1} \\
                                                    &= \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1} \\
                                                    &= \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

where the second line uses the identity $\text{Var}(Av) = A\,\text{Var}(v)\,A^T$ for a fixed matrix $A$; the third line uses $\text{Var}(\varepsilon \mid \mathbf{X}) = \sigma^2 I$, which holds because errors are homoscedastic ($\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2$ for all $i$), mutually uncorrelated ($\text{Cov}(\varepsilon_i, \varepsilon_j) = 0$ for $i \neq j$), and independent of $\mathbf{X}$; and the last line uses $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1} = I$.

$$
\text{Var}_{\mathcal{T}}(\hat{\beta}) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}}\bigl[\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\bigr] = \sigma^2\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}}\bigl[(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\bigr]
$$

Therefore, reversing the sub-lemma and noting that $x_0^T(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}x_0$ depends on $\mathcal{T}$ only through $\mathbf{X}$, so $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}$ on this quantity:

$$
\text{Var}_{\mathcal{T}}(\hat{y}_0) = x_0^T\,\sigma^2\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}}\bigl[(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\bigr]\,x_0 = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}\bigl[x_0^T(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}x_0\bigr]\,\sigma^2 \qquad\square
$$

With these lemmas established, the proof of equation \@ref(eq:epe-linear) proceeds as follows.

*Proof.* Decompose $y_0 - \hat{y}_0$ into three terms that telescope to the full residual:

$$
y_0 - \hat{y}_0 = \underbrace{(y_0 - x_0^T\beta)}_{U_1} + \underbrace{(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[\hat{y}_0] - \hat{y}_0)}_{U_2} + \underbrace{(x_0^T\beta - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[\hat{y}_0])}_{U_3}
$$

One verifies directly that $U_1 + U_2 + U_3 = y_0 - \hat{y}_0$. Squaring and expanding,

$$
(y_0 - \hat{y}_0)^2 = U_1^2 + U_2^2 + U_3^2 + 2U_1U_2 + 2U_1U_3 + 2U_2U_3
$$

Taking $\mathbb{E}_{y_0 \mid x_0}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[\,\cdot\,]$, we evaluate the three diagonal terms. For $U_1^2$: writing $y_0 = x_0^T\beta + \varepsilon_0$ so that $U_1 = \varepsilon_0$,

$$
\mathbb{E}_{y_0 \mid x_0}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[U_1^2] = \mathbb{E}_{y_0 \mid x_0}[(y_0 - x_0^T\beta)^2] = \mathbb{E}_{y_0 \mid x_0}[\varepsilon_0^2] = \text{Var}(\varepsilon_0 \mid x_0) = \sigma^2
$$

where the last equality uses $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_0 \mid x_0] = 0$, the property of conditional mean and $\text{Var}(\varepsilon_0 \mid x_0) = \sigma^2$ by the homoscedasticity assumption. For $U_2^2$:

$$
\mathbb{E}_{y_0 \mid x_0}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[U_2^2] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}\bigl[(\hat{y}_0 - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[\hat{y}_0])^2\bigr] = \text{Var}_{\mathcal{T}}(\hat{y}_0)
$$

For $U_3^2$: by Lemma \@ref(lem:lem-unbiased), $\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[\hat{y}_0] = x_0^T\beta$, and therefore

$$
U_3 = x_0^T\beta - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[\hat{y}_0] = 0
$$

so $\mathbb{E}_{y_0 \mid x_0}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[U_3^2] = 0$. This is the Bias$^2$ term of the decomposition; it vanishes because least squares is unbiased.

It remains to verify that all cross terms vanish. For $2U_1U_2$: by Lemma \@ref(lem:lem-linear-rep), $\hat{y}_0 = x_0^T\beta + \sum_{i}l_i(x_0)\varepsilon_i$, so

$$
U_2 = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[\hat{y}_0] - \hat{y}_0 = x_0^T\beta - \left(x_0^T\beta + \sum_{i=1}^N l_i(x_0)\varepsilon_i\right) = -\sum_{i=1}^N l_i(x_0)\varepsilon_i
$$

Since $U_1 = y_0 - x_0^T\beta$ depends only on the test output $y_0$ and not on the training set $\mathcal{T}$, it factors out of $\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}$:

$$
\mathbb{E}_{y_0 \mid x_0}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[U_1 U_2] = \mathbb{E}_{y_0 \mid x_0}\left[(y_0 - x_0^T\beta)\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}\!\left[-\sum_{i=1}^N l_i(x_0)\varepsilon_i\right]\right]
$$

By linearity and $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i] = 0$ for all $i$:

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}\!\left[-\sum_{i=1}^N l_i(x_0)\varepsilon_i\right] = -\sum_{i=1}^N l_i(x_0)\,\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i] = 0
$$

Hence $\mathbb{E}_{y_0 \mid x_0}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}[U_1U_2] = 0$. The remaining cross terms vanish trivially: since $U_3 = 0$, both $2U_1U_3 = 0$ and $2U_2U_3 = 0$ hold identically.

Combining the three diagonal terms:

$$
\text{EPE}(x_0) = \sigma^2 + \text{Var}_{\mathcal{T}}(\hat{y}_0) + 0 = \sigma^2 + \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}\bigl[x_0^T(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}x_0\bigr]\,\sigma^2 \qquad\square
$$

</details>

### Expected EPE Averaged Over $x_0$

Equation \@ref(eq:epe-linear) shows that the EPE at a fixed $x_0$ depends on both $x_0$ and the random design $\mathbf{X}$. When $N$ is large and $\mathcal{T}$ is drawn at random with $\mathbb{E}[X] = 0$, averaging over $x_0$ yields the linear growth

$$
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}_{x_0}\,\text{EPE}(x_0) \approx \sigma^2\,\frac{p}{N} + \sigma^2
(\#eq:epe-avg)
\end{equation}
$$

<details>
<summary>Proof of expected EPE over $x_0$</summary>

*Proof.* Since $\mathbb{E}[X] = 0$ by assumption, the covariance of $X$ simplifies to

$$
\text{Cov}(X) = \mathbb{E}\bigl[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])(X - \mathbb{E}[X])^T\bigr] = \mathbb{E}[XX^T]
$$

By the law of large numbers applied to the $N$ i.i.d. rows $x_i$ of $\mathbf{X}$:

$$
\frac{\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}}{N} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N x_i x_i^T \;\xrightarrow{N\to\infty}\; \mathbb{E}[XX^T] = \text{Cov}(X)
$$

Writing $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} = N \cdot (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}/N)$ and inverting:

$$
(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1} = \frac{1}{N}\left(\frac{\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}}{N}\right)^{-1} \approx \frac{1}{N}\,\text{Cov}(X)^{-1}
$$

for large $N$. Substituting into equation \@ref(eq:epe-linear):

$$
\text{EPE}(x_0) \approx \sigma^2 + \frac{\sigma^2}{N}\,x_0^T\,\text{Cov}(X)^{-1}\,x_0
$$

Taking expectation over $x_0$, we apply the trace identity: for any square matrix $A$ and vector $x$,

$$
x^TAx = \text{trace}(Axx^T)
$$

This holds because $\text{trace}(Axx^T) = \sum_{i}\sum_j A_{ij}(xx^T)_{ji} = \sum_i\sum_j A_{ij}x_jx_i = x^TAx$. Applying this with $A = \text{Cov}(X)^{-1}$:

$$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\mathbb{E}_{x_0}\bigl[x_0^T\,\text{Cov}(X)^{-1}\,x_0\bigr] &= \mathbb{E}_{x_0}\bigl[\text{trace}\bigl(\text{Cov}(X)^{-1}x_0x_0^T\bigr)\bigr] \\
                                                          &= \text{trace}\bigl(\text{Cov}(X)^{-1}\,\mathbb{E}_{x_0}[x_0 x_0^T]\bigr)
\end{split}
\end{equation}
$$

where the second equality uses the linearity of trace and expectation. Since $\mathbb{E}[X] = 0$, the second moment equals the covariance: $\mathbb{E}_{x_0}[x_0 x_0^T] = \text{Cov}(X)$. Therefore

$$
\text{trace}\bigl(\text{Cov}(X)^{-1}\,\text{Cov}(X)\bigr) = \text{trace}(I_p) = p
$$

Combining with equation \@ref(eq:epe-linear):

$$
\mathbb{E}_{x_0}\,\text{EPE}(x_0) \approx \sigma^2 + \frac{p\,\sigma^2}{N} = \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{p}{N} + 1\right) \qquad\square
$$
</details>

The expected prediction error grows linearly in $p$ at rate $\sigma^2/N$. By imposing the parametric structure $f(x) \approx x^T\beta$, least squares circumvents the curse of dimensionality: the estimation cost scales as $p/N$ rather than exponentially in $p$.

```{r dimsim1, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="Simulation example 1", fig.width=10, fig.height=10}
# X ~ Uniform[-1,1]^p, query point x0 = 0, no noise


# Target functions
f_27 <- function(x) exp(-8 * sum(x^2))       # Fig 2.7: drops sharply from 0
f_28 <- function(x) 0.5 * (x[1] + 1)^3      # Fig 2.8: depends only on x1

# 1-NN Monte Carlo simulation
# Returns MSE, Variance, Bias^2, and average distance to 1-NN at x0 = 0
simulate_1nn <- function(f, p, N = 500, n_sim = 1000) {
  x0   <- rep(0, p)
  f_x0 <- f(x0)
  
  preds <- numeric(n_sim)
  dists <- numeric(n_sim)
  
  for (i in seq_len(n_sim)) {
    X         <- matrix(runif(N * p, -1, 1), nrow = N, ncol = p)
    d         <- sqrt(rowSums(sweep(X, 2, x0, "-")^2))
    nn        <- which.min(d)
    preds[i]  <- f(X[nn, ])
    dists[i]  <- d[nn]
  }
  
  mu <- mean(preds)
  list(
    mse   = mean((preds - f_x0)^2),   # = var + bias2 by bias-variance decomp
    var   = mean((preds - mu)^2),
    bias2 = (mu - f_x0)^2,
    dist  = mean(dists)
  )
}

dims <- 1:10

res_27 <- lapply(dims, function(p) simulate_1nn(f_27, p))
res_28 <- lapply(dims, function(p) simulate_1nn(f_28, p))

extract_df <- function(res) {
  data.frame(
    p     = dims,
    mse   = sapply(res, `[[`, "mse"),
    var   = sapply(res, `[[`, "var"),
    bias2 = sapply(res, `[[`, "bias2"),
    dist  = sapply(res, `[[`, "dist")
  )
}

df_27 <- extract_df(res_27)
df_28 <- extract_df(res_28)

# Figure 2.7

# Training sets
N_disp <- 25
thres <- 0.10
x1d    <- c(thres, runif(N_disp - 1, -1, 1))
# Force no other point closer to 0 than the threshold
x1d[-1] <- ifelse(abs(x1d[-1]) < thres,
                  sign(x1d[-1]) * runif(sum(abs(x1d[-1]) < thres), thres+0.01, 1),
                  x1d[-1])
x2d    <- matrix(runif(N_disp * 2, -1, 1), N_disp, 2)

nn_1d  <- 1                 
nn_2d  <- which.min(sqrt(rowSums(x2d^2)))       # 1-NN to (0,0) in 2D
r_1d   <- abs(x1d[nn_1d])                       # 1D neighborhood radius
r_2d   <- sqrt(sum(x2d[nn_2d, ]^2))             # 2D neighborhood radius

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1), mgp = c(2.5, 0.8, 0))

# Panel 1: 1-NN in One Dimension
xx     <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = 500)
f_nn   <- f_27(x1d[nn_1d])           # predicted value (height at NN)
f_true <- 1                           # f_27(0) = 1

plot(xx, exp(-8 * xx^2), type = "l", col = "green3", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "X", ylab = "f(X)", main = "1-NN in One Dimension",
     ylim = c(-0.03, 1.08))
abline(v = 0, col = "black", lwd = 1)

# Dotted rectangle showing gap between f(x_NN) and f(0)
lines(c(x1d[nn_1d], x1d[nn_1d]), c(0, f_nn), lty = 2, col = "gray40")
lines(c(x1d[nn_1d], 0),          c(f_nn, f_nn), lty = 2, col = "gray40")
lines(c(0, 0),                    c(0, f_true),  lty = 2, col = "gray40")

# Training points as rug; NN in blue, others in red
rug(x1d[-nn_1d], col = "red",  lwd = 1.5, ticksize = 0.03)
rug(x1d[nn_1d],  col = "blue", lwd = 2.5, ticksize = 0.04)

# Highlight NN on curve
points(x1d[nn_1d], f_nn, pch = 19, col = "blue", cex = 0.9)

# Panel 2: 1-NN in One vs. Two Dimensions
plot(x2d, xlab = "X1", ylab = "X2",
     col = "green3", pch = 19, cex = 0.9,
     xlim = c(-1, 1), ylim = c(-1, 1),
     main = "1-NN in One vs. Two Dimensions")

# Orange hatched rectangle: 1D neighborhood (x1 constrained, x2 unconstrained)
rect(-r_1d, -1.05, r_1d, 1.05,
     border = "orange2", lwd = 2, density = 18, angle = 45, col = "orange2")

# Blue hatched circle: 2D neighborhood
theta <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 300)
polygon(r_2d * cos(theta), r_2d * sin(theta),
        border = "blue", lwd = 2, density = 18, angle = 135, col = "blue")

points(0, 0, pch = 19, cex = 1.2)   # query point

# Panel 3: Average Distance to 1-NN vs. Dimension
plot(df_27$p, df_27$dist,
     pch = 19, col = "red", cex = 1.1,
     xlab = "Dimension", ylab = "Average Distance to Nearest Neighbor",
     main = "Distance to 1-NN vs. Dimension",
     ylim = c(0, 1), xaxt = "n")
axis(1, at = dims)

# Dashed linear trend
abline(lm(dist ~ p, data = df_27), lty = 2, col = "red", lwd = 1.5)

# Panel 4: MSE vs. Dimension
ylim4 <- c(0, max(df_27$mse) * 1.05)

plot(df_27$p, df_27$mse, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "red", cex = 1.1,
     xlab = "Dimension", ylab = "MSE", main = "MSE vs. Dimension",
     ylim = ylim4, xaxt = "n")
axis(1, at = dims)
lines(df_27$p, df_27$var,   type = "b", pch = 19, col = "green3", cex = 1.1)
lines(df_27$p, df_27$bias2, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "blue",   cex = 1.1)
legend("topleft",
       legend = c("MSE", "Variance", "Sq. Bias"),
       col    = c("red", "green3", "blue"),
       pch = 19, lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

[^1]: For a detailed proof of the derivation of the normal equation, see Appendix A at the end of this chapter.
[^2]: Proof for $\text{Col}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}) = \text{Col}(\mathbf{X}^T)$ can be accessed at this [Stack Exchange post](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3573576/given-an-n-times-m-matrix-a-prove-that-colata-colat).
[^3]: Derivation of the first-order characterization of a convex function can be accessed at this [pdf file](https://www.princeton.edu/~aaa/Public/Teaching/ORF523/S16/ORF523_S16_Lec7_gh.pdf)
[^4]: If $V$ is a nontrivial linear subspace, then there exists some nonzero vector $v\in V$. As $V$ is closed under scalar multiplication, $cv\in V$ for any scalar $c\in\mathbb{R}$. Since $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable, it follows that $V$ has uncountably many elements.
[^5]: Essentially, the $p$-dim predicted surface generated by the statistical model is determined by the $p$ parameters. A simple linear regression of the form $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1$ forms a line, characterized by ($\beta_0$, $\beta_1$) where all possible values reside. On the other hand, a linear regression of two input variables $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2$ forms a plane, characterized by ($\beta_0$, $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$) where all possible values reside.
[^6]: Generally, the distance metric is specified by the Minkowski distance
    $d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}) = \left(\sum_{r=1}^{N} |x_r - z_r|^p\right)^{1/p}$.
    Special cases include $p = 1$ (Manhattan distance), $p = 2$ (Euclidean distance), and $p \rightarrow \infty$ (Chebyshev distance).
[^7]: Every point in $\mathcal{T}$ but not in $N_k$ is at least as far from $\mathbf{x}$ as the farthest point in $N_k$.
